title: Theory and Toolkits for User Simulation in the Era of Generative AI: User Modeling, Synthetic Data Generation, and System Evaluation
authors: Balog, K.; Zerhoudi, S.; Bernard, N.; Zhai, C.
venue: Proceedings of the 48th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '25)
tldr: A tutorial overview of user simulation methodologies for interactive AI systems, covering behavior models, simulation toolkits, validation methods, and the role of large language models in generating synthetic user interactions.
problem_and_motivation: Rigorously evaluating interactive AI systems, training them with interaction data, and modeling user behavior for personalization remain significant challenges that are difficult to address reproducibly and at scale. Traditional evaluation methods such as test collections, user studies, and A/B testing face limitations in cost, reproducibility, and scalability, particularly with the emergence of generative AI and LLM-powered systems. User simulation offers a versatile methodology to tackle these interconnected issues, but broader adoption is hindered by scarce accessible resources, lack of standardized tools, and skepticism regarding simulation validity.
approach: Synthesizes theoretical foundations of user simulation including behavior models (cognitive, process, strategic) and Markov Decision Processes as a formalism for sequential decision-making.
Covers simulation of specific user interactions: query formulation, result scanning, clicks, effort perception, stopping decisions, and conversational intents.
Reviews open-source toolkits and frameworks such as SimIIR, UserSimCRS, and GenTUS for practical implementation of user simulators.
Discusses validation principles including validity, fidelity, and interpretability, with methods such as distribution matching against real interaction logs and sensitivity analysis.
Highlights the role of large language models as a new generation of simulation approaches for generating synthetic user behavior.
Examines connections between simulation for evaluation, training of interactive systems, and user modeling as deeply interrelated tasks.
findings: Traditional IR metrics like Precision, Recall, and NDCG@k can be interpreted as implicit, naive user models within the simulation framework.
LLM-based simulators represent the newest generation of approaches, enabling zero-shot LLM-to-LLM interaction simulation for conversational QA.
Simulation provides controlled environments crucial for training interactive AI systems and developing nuanced user models.
Broader adoption of user simulation is hindered by scarcity of accessible resources and standardized tools alongside validity skepticism.
Validation methodologies include quantitative comparisons against real user logs, sequence similarity analysis, and task-based evaluation.
Simulation connects evaluation, training, and user modeling as deeply interrelated applications rather than isolated tasks.

definitions.definition: Methodology employing intelligent agents to mimic human interaction patterns with interactive AI systems.
Mathematical framework for formalizing sequential decision-making, widely used for constructing user simulators.
Systems including search engines, recommender systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications that engage users dynamically.
Large Language Model, a class of AI models used for generating synthetic user behavior in simulation.
Degree to which a simulator's behavior closely matches real human interaction patterns.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This tutorial provides a comprehensive synthesis of user simulation methodologies for interactive AI systems, connecting three traditionally separate research threads: system evaluation, algorithm training, and user modeling. It establishes theoretical foundations through behavior models and formalisms while surveying the latest generation of LLM-based simulation approaches. The paper contributes practical guidance by reviewing open-source toolkits, validation methodologies, and benchmark resources, lowering the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners. It also identifies key open challenges including simulation validity, resource scarcity, and the interdisciplinary nature of remaining problems.
